questions.q: English and French colonies in North America were founded during a cool era of harsh winters lasting roughly from the 1300s to the mid-1800s. What do climate historians call it?
questions.explain: The Little Ice Age brought colder winters to the North Atlantic world, and historians link it to hardships at early colonies such as Jamestown and Quebec.

questions.q: In colonial New Spain, the hierarchy that ranked people by their mix of Spanish, Native and African ancestry was known as what?
questions.explain: The casta system placed people of Spanish birth at the top and assigned mixed-ancestry groups such as mestizos and mulattos lower ranks; casta paintings illustrated it.

questions.q: Moundville, one of the largest Mississippian ceremonial centers, with more than two dozen earthen mounds around a great plaza, is in which present-day state?
questions.explain: Moundville, on the Black Warrior River in Alabama, flourished from about 1000 to 1450 and was among the largest Mississippian sites after Cahokia.

questions.q: Paiute and Shoshone peoples of the Great Basin depended heavily on which autumn harvest, gathered from native trees and stored for winter?
questions.explain: Pine nuts from pinyon trees were a key winter food for Great Basin peoples, who moved seasonally among scattered resources in the dry region.

questions.q: Before they had horses, Plains hunters often killed many bison at once by what method?
questions.explain: At buffalo jumps such as Head-Smashed-In in Alberta, hunters drove bison over cliffs and butchered them below.

questions.q: On his second voyage in 1493, Columbus carried which crop to Hispaniola, beginning its spread into the Caribbean?
questions.explain: Columbus brought sugarcane cuttings from the Canary Islands in 1493; sugar plantations later drove the use of enslaved African labor across the Caribbean.

questions.q: In 1542, which explorer sailing for Spain led the first European expedition along the coast of present-day California?
questions.explain: Cabrillo entered San Diego Bay in 1542 and sailed north along the coast; Cabrillo National Monument in San Diego honors him.

questions.q: In 1570, Spanish Jesuits founded the short-lived Ajacan mission, whose missionaries were killed by local Native people within months. Where was it?
options: On the coast of present-day Maine
On the Chesapeake Bay in present-day Virginia
On the Rio Grande in present-day New Mexico
On San Francisco Bay in present-day California
questions.explain: Guided by Paquiquineo (Don Luis), a Native man who had lived in Spain, the Jesuits settled on the Virginia peninsula; the missionaries were killed in early 1571.

questions.q: Santa Elena, a capital of Spanish Florida in the late 1500s, stood in what is now which state?
questions.explain: Founded by Pedro Menendez de Aviles on present-day Parris Island, South Carolina, Santa Elena was abandoned in 1587 as Spain pulled back to St. Augustine.

questions.q: Ancient Hopewell traders of the Ohio Valley obtained copper from which distant region?
questions.explain: The Hopewell exchange network moved Lake Superior copper, Gulf Coast shells and western obsidian across much of the continent.

questions.q: The Chumash of the southern California coast were known for building what?
questions.explain: Chumash tomols, made of planks sewn together and sealed with tar, carried traders and fishermen to the Channel Islands.

questions.q: Maize was domesticated thousands of years ago from teosinte, a wild grass native to which region?
questions.explain: Genetic studies trace maize to teosinte in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago; it later spread across the Americas.

questions.q: The Black Legend, spread by Spain's European rivals, portrayed Spanish colonization as what?
questions.explain: Protestant rivals such as England and the Netherlands used accounts like Las Casas's to depict Spain as especially brutal, a view historians call the Black Legend.

questions.q: Fluted stone spear points used by some of the earliest widespread peoples of North America, roughly 13,000 years ago, are named after a site near which town?
questions.explain: Clovis points were first identified near Clovis, New Mexico, in the 1930s and have been found across much of North America.

questions.q: Among Ancestral Puebloan and later Pueblo peoples, what is a kiva?
options: A chamber used for ceremonies and meetings
A canal dug for irrigating fields of desert maize
A clay jar for storing maize
A trading post for buffalo hides
questions.explain: Kivas, often round and partly underground, were used for religious rituals and community gatherings, and Pueblo communities still use them today.

questions.q: Which Native people lived in northeastern Florida when the Spanish founded St. Augustine in 1565?
questions.explain: Timucua-speaking peoples held much of northern Florida; disease, mission labor and raids nearly destroyed them by the 1700s.

questions.q: Many Native peoples of the eastern woodlands regularly set controlled fires in forests. What was one main purpose?
options: To clear underbrush for hunting and travel
To drive rival villages away during wartime raids
To signal the arrival of European ships
questions.explain: Regular burning opened up forests, improved browse for deer and made travel easier, which early colonists described as park-like woods.

questions.q: Before exploring Florida in 1513, Juan Ponce de Leon had led the Spanish colonization of which Caribbean island?
questions.explain: Ponce de Leon founded the first Spanish settlement on Puerto Rico in 1508 and became its first governor.

questions.q: Mesoamerican cooks soaked maize in an alkaline solution of lime or wood ash before grinding it. What did this process do?
options: Turned the maize into a fermented ceremonial drink
Removed a poison found in raw maize
Made maize more nutritious and easier to grind
questions.explain: Nixtamalization releases niacin and softens the kernels, which helped prevent the disease pellagra in maize-based diets.

questions.q: Columbus sailed south to the Canary Islands before heading west in 1492 in order to use what?
questions.explain: The trade winds blowing from the northeast at that latitude carried his ships west; he returned farther north on the westerlies.

questions.q: Acorns were a staple food for many Native peoples of California. What did cooks have to do before eating them?
options: Leach out bitter tannins with water
Mix them with salt carried from the desert
questions.explain: After grinding acorns into meal, cooks rinsed it repeatedly with water to remove tannins, then made mush or bread.

questions.q: Hernando de Soto's expedition passed through Coosa in 1540. What was Coosa?
options: A powerful Mississippian chiefdom in the Southeast
A Spanish fort on the Gulf Coast
An Inca city in the Andes
A Pueblo town on the Rio Grande
questions.explain: Coosa was a paramount chiefdom centered in northwest Georgia; later Spanish visitors found it much weakened, likely by disease.

questions.q: The Calusa of southwest Florida, who resisted Spanish colonizers in the 1500s, built a powerful chiefdom based mainly on what?
options: Fishing and gathering shellfish in estuaries
questions.explain: The Calusa built shell mounds and canals and supported a complex society on the rich fisheries of the coast without major farming.

questions.q: Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast built large multifamily houses from what material?
questions.explain: Red cedar from the coastal rainforest supplied planks for houses as well as dugout canoes and carved poles.

questions.q: The Mandan and Hidatsa, farming peoples of the upper Missouri River, lived in villages of what kind of dwellings?
questions.explain: Their fortified earth-lodge villages were major trading centers for Plains peoples; Lewis and Clark wintered near them in 1804-1805.

questions.q: In 1729, the Natchez attacked which French post on the lower Mississippi, starting a war in which the French destroyed the Natchez as an independent nation?
questions.explain: The attack at Fort Rosalie, at present-day Natchez, Mississippi, led to French campaigns that killed or enslaved many Natchez and scattered survivors among other nations.

questions.q: The Flushing Remonstrance of 1657 protested New Netherland governor Peter Stuyvesant's persecution of which religious group?
questions.explain: Residents of Flushing on Long Island defended Quakers' freedom of worship, an early American statement of religious liberty.

questions.q: Parliament's Woolen Act of 1699 restricted colonists from doing what?
options: Exporting wool and woolen cloth to other colonies or abroad
questions.explain: The act protected English cloth makers by barring colonial wool and woolen goods from export, an example of mercantilist trade rules.

questions.q: In colonial Virginia and Maryland, what commodity commonly served as money for taxes, debts and ministers' salaries?
questions.explain: Tobacco, and later warehouse receipts for it called tobacco notes, served as currency in the Chesapeake through much of the colonial era.

questions.q: Founded in 1670 with a royal charter, which English company competed with the French for furs across much of northern North America?
questions.explain: The Hudson's Bay Company was given trading rights over the lands draining into Hudson Bay, beginning a long fur rivalry with New France.

questions.q: In 1701, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac founded a French fort and settlement on a strait linking the Great Lakes. Which city grew from it?
questions.explain: Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit controlled the passage between Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie and anchored the French fur trade in the region.

questions.q: In the 1700s, the Comanche built a powerful empire on the southern Plains largely by mastering what?
options: Horses for hunting, raiding and trade
Iron smelting and making their own guns
questions.explain: Mounted Comanche dominated the bison-hunting and horse trade of the southern Plains and held Spanish Texas and New Mexico at bay for decades.

questions.q: By the late 1600s, why did the fur trade in the Hudson and St. Lawrence valleys keep pushing farther west?
options: Beaver fur had gone out of fashion
Spanish forts blocked the eastern rivers
questions.explain: Intense trapping exhausted beaver near the coast, pushing traders and their Native partners west and fueling conflicts such as the Beaver Wars.

questions.q: In 1656, Elizabeth Key won her freedom in a Virginia court partly by arguing what?
options: She had been born in Spain
Her English father was free and she was a baptized Christian
She had served in the militia
She had purchased herself with tobacco
questions.explain: Key's case is thought to have prompted Virginia's 1662 law making a child's status follow the mother's, which made slavery hereditary through the mother.

questions.q: In 1636, minister Thomas Hooker led settlers from Massachusetts Bay to found Hartford in which river valley?
questions.explain: Drawn by fertile land and differences with Massachusetts leaders, Hooker's group settled on the Connecticut River, and the colony adopted the Fundamental Orders in 1639.

questions.q: To boost New France's small population, Louis XIV sponsored the migration of about 800 young women between 1663 and 1673. What were they called?
questions.explain: The filles du roi received royal support to settle and marry in New France, and many French Canadians descend from them.

questions.q: In the Great Peace of Montreal of 1701, the Haudenosaunee agreed to do what?
options: Make peace with New France and its Native allies
questions.explain: The 1701 treaties, signed with about 40 Native nations and France, ended decades of war, while the Haudenosaunee also renewed ties with England and stayed neutral.

questions.q: From 1729 until the early 1770s, the capital of Spanish Texas was Los Adaes, located in what is now which state?
questions.explain: Spain placed its capital at Los Adaes, near present-day Robeline, Louisiana, to guard against the French at nearby Natchitoches.

questions.q: Wall Street in Manhattan takes its name from what?
options: A stone wall around an English fort
A seawall built after a hurricane
A wall the Dutch built at the edge of New Amsterdam
The wall of the first stock exchange
questions.explain: In the 1650s the Dutch built a wooden wall across lower Manhattan for defense; the British tore it down in 1699, and the street along it kept the name.

questions.q: Charles Town, moved to its present site in 1680, grew into a major port at the meeting of which two rivers?
options: The Cape Fear and Neuse rivers
questions.explain: Charleston's peninsula between the Ashley and Cooper rivers offered a protected harbor that made it the leading port of the colonial South.

questions.q: Virginia's Tobacco Inspection Act of 1730 required what?
options: Planters to grow food crops instead of tobacco
All exported tobacco to be inspected at public warehouses
Tobacco to be sold only to Scottish merchants
A tax on tobacco smoked in taverns
questions.explain: Inspectors burned trash tobacco and issued notes for good leaf, which improved quality and circulated as money.

questions.q: Georgia's trustees in the 1730s hoped colonists would produce what luxury good, requiring settlers to plant mulberry trees?
questions.explain: Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves; Georgia's silk industry never became profitable, and rice and later cotton dominated instead.

questions.q: Anthony Johnson, who arrived in Virginia in 1621 as an African servant, is notable for what?
options: Leading a revolt against Governor Berkeley
Becoming a free landowner on the Eastern Shore
Founding the first Black church in America
Serving in the House of Burgesses
questions.explain: Johnson gained his freedom and farmed land on Virginia's Eastern Shore, showing that racial lines in early Virginia were less rigid than they later became.

questions.q: Built in the 1640s, the Saugus Iron Works was the first integrated ironworks in English North America. In which colony was it?
questions.explain: Near Lynn, Massachusetts, it smelted bog iron from 1646 until about 1670 and is now a national historic site.

questions.q: For generations, communities of people who had escaped slavery, called maroons, lived hidden in which swamp on the Virginia-North Carolina border?
questions.explain: Archaeologists have found traces of maroon settlements on islands of higher ground deep in the Great Dismal Swamp, occupied from the 1600s to the Civil War.

questions.q: After the Pequot War, the 1638 Treaty of Hartford did what to the Pequot?
options: Declared their nation dissolved and divided survivors among English allies
Gave them a large reservation in Massachusetts
Moved them west of the Hudson River
questions.explain: Survivors were handed over to the Mohegan and Narragansett or enslaved, and the treaty even banned use of the Pequot name.

questions.q: In 1663, John Eliot published the first complete Bible printed in British North America. In what language was it?
options: Latin, for use by Harvard scholars
Dutch, for settlers in New Netherland colony
questions.explain: Eliot worked with Native translators such as John Sassamon and Cockenoe to produce the Algonquian Bible for missionary work.

questions.q: English philosopher John Locke helped draft the Fundamental Constitutions of 1669 for which colony?
questions.explain: Locke served as secretary to Lord Ashley, one of Carolina's proprietors; the document planned a hereditary nobility and protected slavery.

questions.q: The heavy, boat-shaped Conestoga wagon, used to haul freight in the 1700s and early 1800s, was first built in which colony?
questions.explain: Named for the Conestoga River area of Lancaster County, the wagons carried farm goods to Philadelphia and later freight over the Appalachians.

questions.q: In 1792, two dozen brokers signed an agreement on Wall Street that is considered the origin of what institution?
options: The First Bank of the United States
questions.explain: The Buttonwood Agreement set common commission rates for trading securities, including the new federal bonds created by Hamilton's debt plan.

questions.q: The first U.S. patent, signed by George Washington in 1790, went to Samuel Hopkins for a process of making what?
options: Steam engines for river ships and mills
Potash, used in fertilizer and soap
questions.explain: Under the Patent Act of 1790, Hopkins received the first patent for an improved method of making potash and pearl ash from wood ashes.

questions.q: Hamilton backed the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, chartered in 1791 to build an industrial town at the Great Falls of the Passaic River. Which city grew there?
questions.explain: The society used the falls' water power for mills, and Paterson became a major manufacturing center, later known as the Silk City.

questions.q: In 1763, the Paxton Boys of western Pennsylvania killed which group of Native people, then marched on Philadelphia?
options: Peaceful Conestoga people living near Lancaster
questions.explain: The Paxton Boys murdered about 20 Susquehannock (Conestoga) people; Benjamin Franklin helped persuade the marchers to turn back.

questions.q: The 1785-1786 talks between John Jay and Spain's Diego de Gardoqui angered Westerners because Jay was willing to give up what?
options: Trade with the British West Indies
U.S. navigation of the Mississippi River for years
questions.explain: Jay offered to forgo Mississippi navigation for 25 to 30 years in exchange for trade concessions; Southern states blocked the treaty.

questions.q: Which state, formed from Virginia's western lands, joined the Union in 1792 as the 15th state?
questions.explain: Settlers pouring through the Cumberland Gap made Kentucky the first state west of the Appalachians; Tennessee followed in 1796.

questions.q: In 1784, Grigory Shelikhov founded the first permanent Russian settlement in Alaska on which island?
questions.explain: Shelikhov's post at Three Saints Bay used Alutiiq labor to hunt sea otters for the China fur trade.

questions.q: The 1785 Treaty of Hopewell, signed at a South Carolina plantation, set boundaries between the United States and which Native nation?
questions.explain: The treaty recognized Cherokee lands under U.S. protection, but settlers soon ignored its boundaries.

questions.q: In the 1770s and 1780s, settlers from which colony fought Pennsylvanians for control of the Wyoming Valley along the Susquehanna River?
questions.explain: The Pennamite-Yankee Wars arose from Connecticut's sea-to-sea charter claim; a 1782 court ruling gave the land to Pennsylvania.

questions.q: After Lord Dunmore's War of 1774, the Shawnee agreed to do what?
options: Give up hunting claims south of the Ohio River
Sell the Ohio Country to Virginia
questions.explain: After the Battle of Point Pleasant, the Treaty of Camp Charlotte made the Ohio River the boundary, opening Kentucky to Virginians.

questions.q: The New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-1812, among the strongest ever recorded in the eastern U.S., shook which region?
options: The Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana
questions.explain: Centered near New Madrid, Missouri, the quakes briefly made parts of the Mississippi run backward and helped form Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee.

questions.q: The cold Year Without a Summer of 1816, which ruined New England crops and pushed some farmers west, followed the eruption of which volcano?
questions.explain: Ash from Tambora's 1815 eruption cooled the Northern Hemisphere, bringing June snow to New England and encouraging migration to Ohio and beyond.

questions.q: The Walker Tariff of 1846, passed under President Polk, did what?
questions.explain: Treasury Secretary Robert J. Walker's tariff cut duties toward revenue levels, a Democratic victory that pleased Southern planters.

questions.q: In 1830, Peter Cooper's small steam locomotive Tom Thumb famously raced what on the Baltimore and Ohio line?
questions.explain: The horse won after Tom Thumb's belt slipped, but the trial convinced B&O directors to adopt steam power.

questions.q: Before the factory system, what did merchants do under the putting-out system?
options: Sold western land to settlers on credit
Supplied raw materials to families who made goods at home
Shipped finished goods by canal to Europe
questions.explain: Merchants paid by the piece for spinning, weaving or shoemaking done in homes, a system factories replaced in the early 1800s.

questions.q: John C. Fremont, whose maps and reports of the 1840s guided emigrants to Oregon and California, earned what nickname?
questions.explain: Fremont's expeditions, guided by Kit Carson, were widely read; in 1856 he became the first Republican presidential nominee.

questions.q: In 1824, trapper Jedediah Smith's party crossed the Continental Divide through which broad, gentle gap in present-day Wyoming, later the main wagon route over the Rockies?
questions.explain: Smith's crossing made South Pass widely known; Oregon, California and Mormon Trail emigrants later used it to cross the divide.

questions.q: The Lowell Offering, published in the 1840s, was notable as a magazine written by whom?
options: Enslaved people who had escaped to the North
Young women who worked in the textile mills
questions.explain: Mill workers contributed poems, stories and essays; critics such as Sarah Bagley argued it ignored harsh working conditions.

questions.q: In 1835, workers in which city won a ten-hour day through what is often called the first general strike in North America?
questions.explain: Coal heavers, artisans and laborers joined the walkout, and the city government and many employers agreed to the ten-hour day.

questions.q: In the 1820s to 1840s, New England ships traded manufactured goods to California's ranchos chiefly for what?
questions.explain: Hides became shoe leather in New England mills, a trade described in Richard Henry Dana's Two Years Before the Mast.

questions.q: From 1795 to 1822, the federal government ran trading posts that sold goods to Native peoples at cost. What was this network called?
questions.explain: Government factories aimed to win Native goodwill and undercut private traders, but fur companies lobbied Congress to abolish them in 1822.

questions.q: The Anti-Rent War of 1839-1845 was a tenant revolt against landlords in which region?
options: The Hudson Valley of New York
questions.explain: Tenants on the Van Rensselaer manor and other estates refused to pay rent, and New York's 1846 constitution restricted long-term farm leases.

questions.q: Mexico's Law of April 6, 1830 tried to do what in Texas?
options: Stop further immigration from the United States
Sell Texas to the United States
questions.explain: Alarmed by the growing Anglo-American population, Mexico banned new U.S. immigration to Texas, which angered settlers until Mexico repealed the ban in late 1833 (effective 1834).

questions.q: To cross the Allegheny Mountains, Pennsylvania's Main Line of Public Works, opened in 1834, moved canal boats and cargo over the ridge by what means?
options: A portage railroad with inclined planes
A system of locks over the summit
questions.explain: The Allegheny Portage Railroad used stationary engines to haul cars up and down a series of inclined planes between canal sections.

questions.q: In the 1830s, which artist traveled up the Missouri River painting Plains Indian life and proposed a vast nation's park to protect it?
questions.explain: Catlin painted hundreds of portraits and scenes and in 1832 wrote of preserving the Plains and its peoples in a nation's park.

questions.q: In 1847, Cayuse men killed missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman in Oregon Country, partly blaming them for what?
options: A drought that ruined Cayuse crops
Selling Cayuse land to the British fur traders
A measles epidemic that killed many Cayuse
The murder of a Cayuse chief
questions.explain: Measles carried by emigrants killed about half the Cayuse while white patients often recovered, fueling suspicion of the Whitmans.

questions.q: In 1811-1812, the New Orleans, built by Robert Fulton and Nicholas Roosevelt, became the first steamboat to travel which route?
options: Down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers
Up the Hudson River to Albany
Along the Atlantic coast to Charleston
questions.explain: The boat left Pittsburgh in 1811 and reached New Orleans in January 1812, opening the era of western river steamboats.

questions.q: In 1811, John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company founded which trading post at the mouth of the Columbia River?
questions.explain: Astoria was sold to the British North West Company during the War of 1812 but was later the basis of U.S. claims to Oregon.

questions.q: In 1840, President Martin Van Buren issued an order setting what for laborers on federal public works?
options: A minimum wage of a dollar a day
questions.explain: Van Buren's executive order set a ten-hour day for laborers and mechanics on federal public works.

questions.q: In 1825, Creek leader William McIntosh was executed by order of the Creek National Council for doing what?
options: Signing the Treaty of Indian Springs ceding Creek land
Siding with Britain in the War of 1812
questions.explain: Creek law made selling land without council approval punishable by death; the treaty was later replaced by the 1826 Treaty of Washington.

questions.q: Connecticut clockmaker Eli Terry became known in the early 1800s for what?
options: Building the first American steam locomotive
Mass-producing affordable clocks with interchangeable parts
questions.explain: Terry's water-powered shop turned out thousands of wooden-movement clocks, making clocks common in ordinary homes.

questions.q: John McLoughlin, who aided American settlers arriving in Oregon in the 1840s, ran which Hudson's Bay Company post?
questions.explain: McLoughlin, chief factor at Fort Vancouver on the Columbia, gave supplies and credit to emigrants and is called the Father of Oregon.

questions.q: The 1829 discovery of gold near Dahlonega in north Georgia increased Georgia's pressure to seize land from which Native nation?
questions.explain: The Georgia Gold Rush drew thousands of miners onto Cherokee land, and Georgia distributed the land by lottery before removal.

questions.q: Completed in 1848, the Illinois and Michigan Canal helped make Chicago a hub by linking Lake Michigan with which river system?
questions.explain: The canal ran from the Chicago River to the Illinois River at LaSalle, giving boats a route from the Great Lakes to the Mississippi and the Gulf.

questions.q: In San Francisco, the Chinese Six Companies, a federation of district associations, served Chinese immigrants mainly as what?
options: A railroad company that hired them
A city agency that taxed them
A labor union of white miners
A benevolent group that aided and spoke for them
questions.explain: The Six Companies helped newcomers find work and housing, settled disputes and fought discriminatory laws in court.

questions.q: The Pony Express, which carried mail by relay riders between Missouri and California in 1860 and 1861, was put out of business by what?
options: A federal ban on private mail carriers
questions.explain: The telegraph line linking the coasts was completed in October 1861, and the Pony Express shut down days later.

questions.q: The Department of the Interior, created in 1849, took over the Office of Indian Affairs from which department?
questions.explain: The 1849 act moved Indian affairs from the War Department and the General Land Office from the Treasury into the new department.

questions.q: During the Civil War, British textile mills replaced lost Southern cotton largely with cotton from where?
questions.explain: The cotton famine pushed Britain to buy from India and Egypt, weakening the South's hope that King Cotton would force British recognition.

questions.q: At New York's Crystal Palace exhibition in 1854, Elisha Otis demonstrated a device that later made tall buildings practical. What was it?
questions.explain: Otis had the rope holding his platform cut while he stood on it; his safety catch stopped the fall.

questions.q: Cyrus Field's company laid the first lasting telegraph cable across which body of water in 1866?
questions.explain: An 1858 cable failed within weeks, but the 1866 cable laid by the Great Eastern linked North America and Europe for good.

questions.q: The 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty assigned the Kiowa, Comanche and other southern Plains nations to reservations in which region?
questions.explain: Signed in Kansas, the treaties promised reservations and supplies; later violations led to the Red River War of 1874-1875.

questions.q: Which 1864 law, signed by Lincoln, let employers pay immigrants' passage in exchange for a pledge of future wages, to ease wartime labor shortages?
questions.explain: The act made such labor contracts enforceable and created a federal Commissioner of Immigration; Congress repealed it in 1868.

questions.q: Henry David Thoreau's Walden, published in 1854, describes about two years he spent doing what?
options: Living simply in a cabin by a Massachusetts pond
Traveling through the slave states as a reporter
questions.explain: Thoreau's account of living near Walden Pond outside Concord became a classic of nature writing and simple living.

questions.q: In 1859, Juan Cortina led an armed uprising in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas largely to protest what?
options: Mistreatment of Tejanos and loss of their lands
Mexico's sale of the Gadsden strip
A federal ban on cattle drives
The arrival of the Pony Express
questions.explain: Cortina's forces briefly occupied Brownsville before Texas Rangers and U.S. troops drove them into Mexico.

questions.q: The Page Act of 1875, the first restrictive federal immigration law, was enforced mainly to bar whom?
questions.explain: Aimed at Asian contract laborers and women presumed to be prostitutes, the law sharply cut the arrival of Chinese women years before Chinese exclusion.

questions.q: The Scott Act of 1888 tightened Chinese exclusion by doing what?
options: Requiring a literacy test for all immigrants
Opening Angel Island as a detention station
Barring Chinese laborers who left the U.S. from returning
questions.explain: The act voided return certificates and stranded thousands of Chinese laborers abroad; the Supreme Court upheld it in 1889.

questions.q: The Geary Act of 1892 extended Chinese exclusion and required Chinese residents of the U.S. to do what?
options: Pay a monthly tax to work in the mines
questions.explain: Those without certificates faced deportation; the Supreme Court upheld the law in Fong Yue Ting v. United States (1893).

questions.q: In Yick Wo v. Hopkins (1886), the Supreme Court overturned convictions under a San Francisco laundry ordinance because officials had done what?
options: Passed it without a public vote
Enforced it in a way that discriminated against Chinese owners
Used it to tax interstate trade
questions.explain: The Court held that a law fair on its face but applied unequally violated the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause, even for noncitizens.

questions.q: Before Ellis Island opened, most immigrants arriving in New York from 1855 to 1890 were processed at which station run by New York State?
questions.explain: Castle Garden, in an old fort at the Battery in Manhattan, received more than 8 million immigrants before federal control and Ellis Island.

questions.q: The Immigration Act of 1891 changed who controlled immigration by doing what?
options: Creating a federal immigration office in the Treasury Department
Placing it under the War Department
questions.explain: The act created the Office of the Superintendent of Immigration, and the federal Ellis Island station opened in 1892.

questions.q: In Elk v. Wilkins (1884), the Supreme Court ruled what about John Elk, a Native American who had left his tribe and lived in Omaha?
options: The Fourteenth Amendment did not make him a citizen
He had a right to vote under the Fifteenth Amendment
He had to return to his reservation
He could not own property in Nebraska
questions.explain: The Court held that Native Americans born under tribal authority were not citizens by birth; Congress made all Native Americans citizens in 1924.

questions.q: After Ex parte Crow Dog (1883) held that federal courts could not try a killing of one Lakota by another on a reservation, Congress responded with which law?
questions.explain: The Major Crimes Act of 1885 gave federal courts jurisdiction over murder and other serious crimes among Native people on reservations.

questions.q: In 1887, Theodore Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell founded which club of hunters that pushed for wildlife and park protection?
questions.explain: The club lobbied for protecting Yellowstone and for the Forest Reserve Act of 1891.

questions.q: In 1894, which state amended its constitution to require that its forest preserve lands be kept forever wild?
questions.explain: The forever wild clause protects state lands in the Adirondack and Catskill parks from logging and sale.

questions.q: The Carey Act of 1894 encouraged irrigation of western desert land by doing what?
options: Giving federal land to states that arranged for its irrigation
Building federal dams on the Colorado River
Paying farmers to leave land unplowed
questions.explain: Each western state could receive up to a million acres if it saw to irrigation and settlement; few projects succeeded before the 1902 Reclamation Act.

questions.q: After decades of commercial hide hunting, how many American bison were left by about 1889, from herds once numbering in the tens of millions?
questions.explain: Naturalist William Hornaday counted roughly a thousand bison in 1889, and he later helped found the American Bison Society to save them.

questions.q: Created by Congress in 1879, the Mississippi River Commission was charged with what?
options: Regulating railroad rates in the valley
Improving navigation and flood control on the river
questions.explain: Led by Army engineers and civilians, the commission built levees under a levees-only policy until the 1927 flood forced changes.

questions.q: The Specie Resumption Act of 1875 promised that, starting in 1879, the government would do what?
questions.explain: Resumption put the U.S. back on a gold basis, angering debtors who wanted more money in circulation.

questions.q: Because the Southern Farmers' Alliance excluded Black members, Black farmers formed which organization in 1886?
questions.explain: Founded in Texas, the Colored Farmers' Alliance grew to many thousands of members and cooperated uneasily with white Populists.

questions.q: In the post-Reconstruction South, what did the convict-lease system do?
options: Let prisoners buy their freedom with wages
Sent convicts to settle western land
Rented prisoners, mostly Black, to private companies as laborers
Paid states to build new prisons
questions.explain: States leased convicts to railroads, mines and plantations under brutal conditions; Alabama was the last to end the practice, in 1928.

questions.q: Founded in 1866 under leaders such as William Sylvis, which was the first national federation of American labor unions?
options: The Industrial Workers of the World
questions.explain: The National Labor Union pushed for an eight-hour day and helped win one for federal workers in 1868 before fading in the early 1870s.

questions.q: Rural Free Delivery, begun on a trial basis in 1896, changed farm life by doing what?
options: Building free paved roads to every farm
Bringing mail directly to farm homes
questions.explain: Before RFD, farm families had to fetch mail in town; home delivery boosted newspapers and mail-order catalogs.

questions.q: In 1886, the strongest earthquake recorded in the southeastern U.S. heavily damaged which city?
questions.explain: The August 1886 quake killed dozens of people and damaged many of Charleston’s buildings.

questions.q: After the Great Blizzard of March 1888 paralyzed New York City, which changes did the disaster help spur?
options: Burying utility wires and moving transit underground
Moving the state capital to Albany
questions.explain: Snapped overhead wires and stalled elevated trains pushed officials to bury lines and strengthened the case for underground transit; New York’s first subway opened in 1904.

questions.q: Who was the first immigrant processed at Ellis Island when it opened on January 1, 1892?
options: Emma Lazarus, a poet from New York
Annie Moore, a teenager from Ireland
Jacob Riis, a reporter from Denmark
Andrew Carnegie, a boy from Scotland
questions.explain: Annie Moore of County Cork, arriving with her two brothers, received a ten-dollar gold coin as the first person processed.

questions.q: The McKinley Tariff of 1890 hurt Hawaii's planters by doing what?
options: Erasing the duty-free advantage of Hawaiian sugar
questions.explain: By letting all raw sugar in duty-free and paying U.S. growers a bounty, the tariff wiped out Hawaii's treaty edge and pushed planters toward annexation.

questions.q: George Westinghouse's 1869 invention, which let engineers stop a whole train at once, was what?
questions.explain: Air brakes made longer, faster trains safer, and the Railroad Safety Appliance Act of 1893 made them standard.

questions.q: Built in 1885, which Chicago building is often called the first skyscraper because it used a load-bearing metal frame?
questions.explain: Designed by William Le Baron Jenney, the ten-story Home Insurance Building used iron and steel framing to carry its weight.

questions.q: Las Gorras Blancas, night riders in northern New Mexico around 1889-1890, cut fences to protest what?
options: Anglo ranchers and speculators fencing off Hispano common lands
questions.explain: The White Caps defended village grazing lands granted under Spain and Mexico against enclosure by newcomers.

questions.q: The Timber and Stone Act of 1878 let individuals buy up to 160 acres of what kind of western land at $2.50 an acre?
options: Land unfit for farming but valuable for timber or stone
questions.explain: Timber companies often hired people to file claims and then took over the land, gaining vast forests cheaply.

questions.q: The General Mining Act of 1872 allowed prospectors to do what on federal public land?
options: Mine only after paying high royalties
Stake claims and buy mineral land at low fixed prices
Lease mines for no more than five years
questions.explain: The law let citizens claim land containing valuable minerals and buy it for $2.50 or $5 an acre, without royalties to the government.

questions.q: In 1891, a mob in New Orleans lynched 11 men of which immigrant group after a jury acquitted some of them in the killing of the police chief?
questions.explain: The killings caused a diplomatic crisis with Italy, and the U.S. paid an indemnity to the victims' families.

questions.q: In Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903), the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could do what?
options: Not reduce reservations without unanimous tribal consent
Override treaties with Native nations without their consent
Hand reservations over to state control
Never tax land held by Native people
questions.explain: The Kiowa leader Lone Wolf challenged the sale of reservation land; the Court held Congress had plenary power over Indian affairs.

questions.q: The Burke Act of 1906 changed the Dawes Act by doing what?
options: Ending allotment and restoring tribal lands
Giving all Native Americans the vote
Delaying citizenship until allottees received full title to land
Banning the sale of allotted land
questions.explain: Citizenship waited until the trust period ended, but officials could grant early title to Native people judged competent, which sped land loss.

questions.q: Along with a literacy test, the Immigration Act of 1917 created what?
options: An Asiatic Barred Zone excluding most immigrants from Asia
questions.explain: Congress passed the act over Woodrow Wilson's veto; the barred zone covered much of Asia and the Pacific islands.

questions.q: In Takao Ozawa v. United States (1922), the Supreme Court ruled that Ozawa, a Japanese immigrant, could not become a citizen for what reason?
options: He had lived in the U.S. less than five years
He had joined a labor union
He was not white under the naturalization law
He had served in Japan's army
questions.explain: Though Ozawa had lived in the U.S. for about 20 years, the Court held that only free white persons and people of African descent could naturalize.

questions.q: The Keating-Owen Act of 1916 tried to limit child labor by doing what?
options: Banning interstate sale of goods made by young children
Requiring all children to attend school until age sixteen
Setting a federal minimum wage for teenagers
Giving states money to inspect factories
questions.explain: The Supreme Court struck the law down in Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918), ruling that Congress had overstepped its commerce power.

questions.q: In the 1914 Ludlow Massacre, National Guard troops attacked a tent colony of striking coal miners and their families in which state?
questions.explain: About two dozen people, including women and children, died at the camp of strikers against the Rockefeller-owned Colorado Fuel and Iron Company.

questions.q: What did the Norris-La Guardia Act of 1932 do for organized labor?
options: Barred yellow-dog contracts and most federal court injunctions against strikes
Created the National Labor Relations Board
Allowed states to ban the closed shop
questions.explain: Yellow-dog contracts had made workers promise not to join unions; the act ended their enforcement in federal courts.

questions.q: In the 1937 Memorial Day Massacre, Chicago police killed ten people during a strike against which steel company?
questions.explain: Police fired on marchers supporting the Little Steel strike; U.S. Steel had already recognized the steelworkers' union that year.

questions.q: Created in 1933, which New Deal agency drew residential security maps that shaded many Black and immigrant neighborhoods red as risky?
questions.explain: The HOLC refinanced home mortgages, and its color-coded maps helped spread the practice later called redlining.

questions.q: In Buchanan v. Warley (1917), the Supreme Court struck down what?
options: A city law zoning neighborhoods by race
Private racial covenants written into home deeds
questions.explain: The Court ruled that Louisville's residential segregation ordinance violated property rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.

questions.q: The Transportation Act of 1920 (Esch-Cummins Act) did what?
options: Returned the railroads to private owners after wartime federal control
questions.explain: The government had run the railroads during World War I; the act returned them and gave the ICC power over rates and mergers.

questions.q: When Congress repealed Chinese exclusion with the Magnuson Act of 1943, what annual quota did it set for Chinese immigrants?
questions.explain: The tiny quota showed the repeal was mainly a wartime gesture to China, though Chinese immigrants could now naturalize.

questions.q: The War Brides Act of 1945 allowed whom to enter the U.S. outside normal immigration quotas?
options: Foreign spouses and children of U.S. servicemen
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of spouses, mostly from Europe, came under the act; a 1947 amendment eased entry for Asian spouses.

questions.q: Which 1948 law admitted Europeans uprooted by World War II, such as Holocaust survivors and refugees from Soviet-controlled lands?
questions.explain: Truman criticized the original act as discriminatory, but with later amendments it admitted about 400,000 people.

questions.q: The McCarran-Walter Act of 1952, passed over Truman's veto, did what?
options: Granted legal status to undocumented workers
Ended racial bars to naturalization but kept national origins quotas
questions.explain: The act removed all remaining racial bars, letting Japanese and other Asian immigrants naturalize, while adding grounds to exclude suspected subversives.

questions.q: After the Soviet Union crushed a 1956 uprising, tens of thousands of refugees from which country were received at Camp Kilmer, New Jersey?
questions.explain: Eisenhower used the parole power to admit many of the refugees quickly, a precedent for later refugee crises.

questions.q: Public Law 280 of 1953, part of the termination era, did what?
options: Gave certain states criminal jurisdiction over reservations
questions.explain: The law transferred jurisdiction to states such as California and Minnesota without tribal consent, which tribes long opposed.

questions.q: The Menominee of Wisconsin, whose federal recognition was terminated in the 1950s, regained it in 1973. Which activist led the restoration campaign?
questions.explain: Deer's group DRUMS fought termination, and she later became the first woman to head the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

questions.q: The Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 responded to what problem?
options: Native children being barred from public schools
Large numbers of Native children being placed with non-Native families
A lack of hospitals on reservations
questions.explain: Studies found a quarter to a third of Native children had been removed from their homes, and the act gave tribes a say in placements.

questions.q: Critics of urban renewal under the Housing Act of 1949 charged that it did what?
options: Paid farmers to move to cities
Bulldozed poor and minority neighborhoods and displaced residents
questions.explain: Title I funded slum clearance, but many cleared areas got offices or highways instead of enough new housing for those displaced.

questions.q: Pruitt-Igoe, a huge public housing complex whose demolition began in 1972, became a symbol of the failure of high-rise public housing in which city?
questions.explain: Completed in the mid-1950s, the 33 towers declined quickly from poor upkeep and segregation, and all were torn down by 1976.

questions.q: The Landrum-Griffin Act of 1959, passed after Senate hearings into union corruption, required what?
options: Union financial reports and secret-ballot officer elections
questions.explain: Hearings by the McClellan Committee, with Robert Kennedy as counsel, exposed racketeering in unions such as the Teamsters.

questions.q: In TVA v. Hill (1978), the Supreme Court halted completion of the Tellico Dam to protect which endangered species?
questions.explain: The Court read the Endangered Species Act strictly; Congress later exempted the dam, which was completed in 1979.

questions.q: The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 did what?
options: Gave legal status to about 2.7 million people
Ended the national origins quota system
Expanded grounds for deportation and set multiyear reentry bars
questions.explain: The law also expedited removal at the border and barred people unlawfully present for over a year from returning for ten years.

questions.q: After California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians (1987) limited state power over tribal gaming, Congress passed which law in 1988?
options: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act
questions.explain: The act set up the National Indian Gaming Commission and required tribal-state compacts for casino gaming.

questions.q: In McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020), the Supreme Court ruled that, for federal criminal law, a large area of eastern Oklahoma including much of Tulsa remains what?
options: Reservation land of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation
questions.explain: Justice Gorsuch wrote that Congress had never disestablished the Creek reservation, so major crimes there by Native people fall under federal or tribal courts.

questions.q: In Kelo v. City of New London (2005), the Supreme Court upheld a city's use of eminent domain to do what?
options: Clear land for a military base
Take private homes for a private economic development plan
questions.explain: The 5-4 ruling caused a backlash, and many states then passed laws limiting such takings.

questions.q: In Massachusetts v. EPA (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that the EPA had authority under the Clean Air Act to regulate what?
options: Greenhouse gas emissions from new motor vehicles
questions.explain: The 5-4 decision held that carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases count as air pollutants under the act.

questions.q: In Sackett v. EPA (2023), the Supreme Court narrowed which wetlands are covered by which federal law?
questions.explain: The Court held that the act covers only wetlands with a continuous surface connection to larger regulated waters.

questions.q: The 1994 Northridge earthquake, which killed dozens of people and collapsed freeway bridges, struck which metropolitan area?
questions.explain: The magnitude 6.7 quake hit the San Fernando Valley and caused billions of dollars in damage across the region.

questions.q: Hurricane Andrew in 1992 devastated which area, leading to much stricter building codes there?
questions.explain: Andrew destroyed tens of thousands of homes in Miami-Dade County, including much of Homestead.

questions.q: The 2018 Camp Fire, the deadliest wildfire in California history, largely destroyed which town?
questions.explain: The fire killed 85 people and destroyed nearly 19,000 buildings in Butte County.

questions.q: In 1995 and 1996, federal biologists reintroduced which predator to Yellowstone National Park?
questions.explain: Wolves had been wiped out in the park by the 1920s; 31 wolves captured in Canada were released there in 1995 and 1996.

questions.q: In 1987, the last wild members of which endangered bird were captured for a breeding program, before captive-bred birds were released starting in 1992?
questions.explain: Only 27 condors remained when the last wild one was captured; breeding programs have since restored hundreds.

questions.q: The bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list in 2007. A main cause of its earlier decline was which pesticide, banned in the U.S. in 1972?
questions.explain: DDT thinned eagle eggshells so they broke; after the ban and protection, eagle numbers recovered.

questions.q: Which 2022 law, signed by Joe Biden, contained the largest federal investment in climate and clean energy up to that time?
options: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
questions.explain: It offered tax credits for renewable power, electric vehicles and home efficiency, and passed the Senate with a tie-breaking vote by Vice President Harris.

questions.q: Which 2002 law, passed after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, tightened accounting and auditing rules for public companies?
questions.explain: The act made top executives certify financial reports and created a board to oversee auditors.

questions.q: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by about what share in a single day?
questions.explain: It remains the largest one-day percentage drop in the Dow's history; computerized program trading worsened the selling.

questions.q: In the 1985 Plaza Accord, the U.S. and four other leading economies agreed to do what?
options: Push down the value of the U.S. dollar
questions.explain: Signed at New York's Plaza Hotel, the accord aimed to shrink U.S. trade deficits by making American exports cheaper.

questions.q: In 1984, an antitrust settlement broke up which company's nationwide telephone monopoly into regional Baby Bells?
questions.explain: The settlement of the government's antitrust suit split off seven regional companies, while AT&T kept long distance.

questions.q: In Janus v. AFSCME (2018), the Supreme Court ruled that public-sector unions could not do what?
options: Collect fees from workers who chose not to join
Go on strike in any state
questions.explain: The Court overturned a 1977 precedent, holding that mandatory agency fees violated nonmembers' free speech rights.

questions.q: In Arizona v. United States (2012), the Supreme Court struck down three of four challenged parts of Arizona's 2010 immigration law, SB 1070, on what grounds?
options: They were ex post facto laws
questions.explain: The Court let stand the provision requiring officers to check immigration status during lawful stops.

questions.q: In Trump v. Hawaii (2018), the Supreme Court upheld what?
options: A ban on refugees from Central America
A proclamation restricting entry from several mostly Muslim-majority countries
A wall along the Mexican border
questions.explain: The 5-4 ruling held that the president had broad statutory power to suspend entry of foreign nationals.

questions.q: In 1983, the federal government bought out and evacuated the entire town of Times Beach, Missouri, because its roads had been sprayed with oil contaminated by what?
questions.explain: The town was disincorporated, and the site was cleaned up under the Superfund program and later became a state park.

questions.q: Hurricane Maria in 2017 caused an island-wide power outage lasting months and spurred migration to the mainland from where?
questions.explain: Maria struck as a powerful Category 4 storm, and thousands of deaths were later linked to it.

questions.q: In 2017, which hurricane stalled over the Houston area and set a U.S. record for rainfall from a single tropical storm?
questions.explain: Harvey dropped about 60 inches of rain in places, flooding much of Houston.

questions.q: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 created the Renewable Fuel Standard, requiring gasoline to be blended with fuels such as which one?
questions.explain: The mandate, expanded in 2007, made ethanol a major use of the U.S. corn crop.

questions.q: In United States v. Microsoft (decided 2000-2001), courts found the company had illegally kept a monopoly in which market?
options: Internet search engines and online advertising
questions.explain: An appeals court upheld the monopoly finding but overturned a breakup order, and the case was settled in 2001.
